stem: A patient develops lip and tongue swelling a month after starting lisinopril. Best step?
why: Angioedema is rare but life-threatening — stop the drug.
takeaway: Cough → switch to ARB; angioedema → stop.
discriminator: Bradykinin accumulation drives both.

stem: Why do loop diuretics raise urinary calcium while thiazides lower it?

options.A: Thiazides block NKCC2 in the loop

why: NKCC2 block collapses the lumen-positive potential that drives paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ reabsorption; thiazides lower cell Na⁺ so NCX reabsorbs more Ca²⁺.
takeaway: Loops lose calcium; thiazides take it back.
discriminator: Thiazides help calcium stones and osteoporosis; loops help hypercalcemia.

stem: Why are ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferred in proteinuric CKD?

options.B: They are the only class allowed
options.E: They lower BP more than any class

why: Less angiotensin II dilates the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria — renoprotection beyond BP.
takeaway: Similar BP lowering; ACEi/ARBs add renoprotection.
discriminator: The same action explains the creatinine rise.

stem: A woman with hypertension, normal renal function and recurrent calcium kidney stones needs a diuretic. Which fits best?
why: Thiazides decrease calcium excretion — first-line HTN and helpful for calcium stones.
discriminator: Textbook: add fluid, cut salt, don’t restrict dietary calcium.

stem: A week after starting losartan, creatinine rose 45% with a soft BP. What should be evaluated?
why: Up to ~30% is expected; a larger rise warrants checking for volume depletion or renal artery stenosis.
takeaway: Thirty is fine, more is a sign.
discriminator: Bilateral renal artery stenosis is a contraindication.

stem: How do nitrates relieve angina?
why: Nitric oxide activates guanylate cyclase, raising cGMP; venodilation reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand.
takeaway: Nitrates = preload; DHP CCBs = afterload; BB/non-DHP = heart rate.
discriminator: Nitrate-free interval prevents tolerance.

stem: Which electrolyte pattern do loop diuretics produce?
why: Loops: hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia, ototoxicity.
discriminator: Hypokalemia raises digoxin toxicity.

stem: A patient on spironolactone is prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Main concern?
why: Potassium supplements and trimethoprim add hyperkalemia with potassium-sparing diuretics.
takeaway: K⁺-sparing + anything that holds K⁺ → check K⁺.
discriminator: Also ACEi/ARB and CKD.

stem: A patient on lisinopril asks what to do during a bout of vomiting and diarrhea. Best advice?

options.A: Double the dose to protect the kidney

why: Sick-day rules: hold ACEi/ARB during volume depletion — reduced perfusion plus RAAS blockade can precipitate AKI.
discriminator: Same principle drives the triple whammy.

stem: A patient’s chlorthalidone stops controlling BP as eGFR falls to 24 mL/min. What change fits best?
why: Thiazides lose efficacy below GFR ~30; a loop acts upstream and still works.
discriminator: Same logic explains many cases of resistant hypertension in CKD.

stem: A man with stable angina asks whether he can use sildenafil. He carries nitroglycerin. Best answer?

options.A: Yes, if doses are 6 hours apart
options.B: Only if he also takes a beta-blocker

why: PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown; with nitrates, life-threatening hypotension — an absolute contraindication.
discriminator: One of the highest-stakes safety points in the unit.

stem: Which drug blocks the RAAS at the step that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II?
why: ACE inhibitors (-pril) block angiotensin I → II; ARBs block AT1; aliskiren blocks renin; spironolactone blocks aldosterone.
takeaway: Renin → ACE → AT1 → aldosterone: four blockers, four steps.
discriminator: Angiotensin II drives vasoconstriction and aldosterone release.

stem: Why is hydralazine given with a beta-blocker and a diuretic?
why: Direct arteriolar dilation triggers reflex tachycardia and salt and water retention.
discriminator: Clonidine: rebound hypertension if stopped abruptly.

stem: A patient on valsartan and furosemide has back pain. Which pain reliever plan is safest per the lecture?
why: On a RAAS blocker and diuretic, avoid regular NSAIDs and ask before any OTC product.
takeaway: RAAS blocker + diuretic → no routine NSAIDs.
discriminator: The preventable element is what the patient was told.

stem: Why must a renally cleared drug be adjusted when GFR falls?

options.B: It is cleared faster in CKD
options.D: Its loading dose must always double
options.E: Its oral absorption falls along with GFR

why: Reduced GFR causes accumulation; reduce the dose, extend the interval, or both.

whys.A: Parent drug and active metabolites both matter.

discriminator: Maintenance doses get adjusted; loading doses often don’t.
src: L09 S5; S6; S8; SG U5-R1

stem: What is the most common adverse effect of nitrates, and why?
why: Nitrate adverse effects: headache (vasodilation), reflex tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension.
discriminator: Tolerance → nitrate-free interval.

stem: A patient on amlodipine has ankle swelling without heart failure. Most likely cause?
why: Peripheral edema is a CCB class adverse effect, especially dihydropyridines.
discriminator: Non-DHPs: bradycardia, constipation.

stem: An older woman on hydrochlorothiazide is confused with sodium 121 mEq/L. Which statement fits?
why: Thiazide hyponatremia can be significant, especially in older adults.
discriminator: Loops are, if anything, protective against hyponatremia (textbook).

stem: A patient on isosorbide mononitrate twice daily, around the clock, reports angina returning. Likely cause?
why: Continuous exposure causes tolerance; a nitrate-free interval (typically overnight) maintains efficacy.
discriminator: Isosorbide dinitrate profile: 14-hour nitrate-free interval.

stem: Which component of the triple whammy constricts the afferent arteriole?
why: NSAID afferent constriction + ACEi/ARB efferent dilation + diuretic volume depletion each lower filtration pressure.
discriminator: Counsel on OTC NSAIDs.

stem: A drug’s toxic effect tracks its peak level, and kidney function has fallen. Which lever is described on the slides?

options.A: Add a second renally cleared drug

why: Reduce the maintenance dose when the effect is concentration-dependent; extend the interval when the half-life is long.
discriminator: Monitor after each change.

stem: A patient with decompensated heart failure has raised intracranial pressure. Why is mannitol risky?
why: Mannitol pulls water into the extracellular space before diuresis — can worsen volume overload; avoid in heart failure.
takeaway: Mannitol: ICP/IOP; needs renal perfusion; not in heart failure.
discriminator: Monitor osmolality and electrolytes.

stem: Creatinine rises from 1.2 to 1.5 mg/dL two weeks after starting losartan. What next?
why: A rise up to ~30% reflects reduced intraglomerular pressure; a larger rise suggests renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
takeaway: Thirty is fine, more is a sign.
discriminator: Check K⁺ and creatinine in 1–2 weeks.
src: L10 S5; S9; S10; SG U5-R9

stem: A climber plans a rapid ascent above 3000 m next week. Which drug and timing fit?

options.E: Mannitol IV once at the summit

why: Acetazolamide 125–250 mg BID starting a day before ascent; it blocks Na⁺/HCO₃⁻ reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
discriminator: Predictable adverse effect: metabolic acidosis.

stem: A stage 3 CKD patient on lisinopril starts spironolactone; two weeks later K⁺ is 6.1 mEq/L. Best explanation?
why: ACE inhibitor lowers aldosterone, spironolactone blocks its receptor, and CKD limits K⁺ excretion — risk compounds.
discriminator: Check K⁺ and creatinine within 1 week of starting spironolactone.

stem: A patient on verapamil starts digoxin for atrial fibrillation. What should be anticipated?
why: Verapamil and diltiazem raise digoxin levels.
discriminator: Non-DHP + beta-blocker → AV block.

stem: A patient on digoxin starts high-dose furosemide for edema. Which lab change most raises digoxin toxicity?
why: Hypokalemia from loops increases digoxin toxicity.
discriminator: Aminoglycosides add ototoxicity with loops.

stem: An 82-year-old on several renally cleared drugs is admitted with vomiting and dehydration. What is the best dosing habit?

options.A: Adjust only the antibiotics, nothing else
options.B: Keep doses based on last year’s labs
options.E: Double every loading dose to be safe

why: Reassess as renal function changes — acute illness, dehydration or nephrotoxic drugs can drop GFR quickly.
takeaway: Check CrCl or eGFR before dosing, and again when the patient gets sick.
discriminator: Examples needing adjustment: vancomycin, beta-lactams, digoxin, DOACs, metformin.

stem: Which statement about potassium-sparing diuretics is correct?

options.D: Both cause hypokalemia, like the loops do
options.E: Both block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb

why: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) vs. ENaC blockers (amiloride, triamterene); shared risk hyperkalemia.
takeaway: Block the hormone or block the channel.
discriminator: Spironolactone is antiandrogen; eplerenone mostly isn’t.

stem: A patient on lithium starts hydrochlorothiazide. What should be anticipated?
why: Thiazides raise lithium levels — monitor closely.
discriminator: NSAIDs blunt diuretic effect.

stem: How should a patient on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic be counseled about pain relievers?

options.A: NSAIDs are safe because they are OTC
options.B: Take NSAIDs with extra water only
options.C: Double the diuretic when using NSAIDs
options.D: Stop the ACE inhibitor on pain days
options.E: Avoid NSAIDs; ask before any OTC

why: Prevention requires counseling to avoid regular NSAID use and to check with a prescriber or pharmacist before any OTC product.
takeaway: The preventable element is what the patient was told.
discriminator: Ask which OTC NSAIDs they already take.

stem: A patient’s chest pain persists 5 minutes after one sublingual nitroglycerin. Per the profile, what next?
why: Acute angina: 0.4 mg SL every 5 minutes up to 3 doses.
takeaway: SL nitro: up to 3 doses, 5 minutes apart.
discriminator: Sublingual bypasses first-pass.

stem: A patient with gout and hypertension is starting a diuretic. Which class most worsens gout?
why: Thiazides cause hyperuricemia and can precipitate gout (they compete for uric acid secretion).
discriminator: Loops also raise uric acid.

stem: A patient with acute angle-closure concerns and high intraocular pressure needs a systemic agent before surgery. Which diuretic lowers IOP?
why: Mannitol lowers raised intraocular and intracranial pressure; acetazolamide lowers aqueous humor production.
discriminator: Avoid mannitol in heart failure.

stem: CKD with eGFR 27 mL/min; BP above goal on lisinopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. First change?
why: Resistant HTN in CKD is often a diuretic-selection problem: at this GFR HCTZ has lost efficacy; switch to furosemide or torsemide.
takeaway: Check the diuretic before adding a class.
discriminator: Then spironolactone with close K⁺ monitoring.

stem: A patient on enalapril has a persistent dry cough. What is the best change?
why: ACE-inhibitor cough is bradykinin-mediated; ARBs don’t raise bradykinin, so they are the usual switch.
discriminator: Cough is the most common reason to switch.

stem: A patient on metoprolol develops second-degree AV block after a new BP drug. Which drug was added?
why: Non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) plus a beta-blocker → bradycardia and AV block.
discriminator: DHPs act on arterioles, not the AV node.

stem: A 28-year-old with proteinuric CKD plans pregnancy next year. What must be discussed before an ACE inhibitor?
why: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal renal toxicity).
discriminator: Methyldopa is the pregnancy option on the slides.

stem: A man with heart failure developed gynecomastia on spironolactone. Which substitute fits best?
why: Eplerenone is selective and largely avoids spironolactone’s antiandrogen effects; avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
discriminator: Eplerenone + ketoconazole → levels rise sharply.

stem: Where is the most potent diuretic target located?
why: Loops block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb (~25% of filtered sodium).
takeaway: Potency follows the share of sodium reabsorbed.
discriminator: Loops stay effective in advanced CKD.

stem: A patient will receive IV furosemide for pulmonary edema. Which administration rule prevents ototoxicity?

options.A: Give it as a rapid push
options.C: Give double the oral dose IV

why: Ototoxicity occurs with rapid IV or high doses; give IV furosemide no faster than 4 mg/min.
discriminator: Usually reversible (textbook).

stem: An older adult on lisinopril and HCTZ starts daily OTC naproxen; a week later creatinine is up acutely. Mechanism?
why: NSAID afferent constriction + ACEi efferent dilation + diuretic volume depletion combine additively to synergistically → AKI.
discriminator: At eGFR 25, also switch HCTZ to a loop.
src: L10 S23; S27; SG U5-R12; SG U5-S

stem: When GFR falls, which dose is usually unchanged for a renally cleared drug?
why: Loading doses depend on volume of distribution and are often unchanged; maintenance doses are adjusted.
discriminator: Reassess when GFR changes.

stem: Which class treats both hypertension and angina by the same mechanism?
why: Arteriolar dilation reduces afterload — lowering BP and myocardial oxygen demand.
discriminator: Non-DHPs also slow the heart and raise coronary flow.

stem: A patient on lithium develops nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Which diuretic is used?
why: Amiloride blocks lithium entry into collecting-duct cells and treats lithium-induced NDI; thiazides also help.
discriminator: Monitor lithium levels with diuretics.

stem: Which pairing of diuretic class and nephron site is correct?
why: Loop TAL; thiazide DCT; K⁺-sparing collecting duct; CAI proximal tubule; osmotic throughout (mainly proximal).

whys.C: Loops act at the thick ascending limb.

takeaway: Site predicts potency and electrolyte effects.
discriminator: Na⁺ reabsorbed: PT ~65%, TAL ~25%, DCT 5–8%, CD 2–3%.
src: L09 S7; SG U5-R2; SG U5-M

stem: A patient with CKD and resistant hypertension is already on a loop diuretic, ACEi and CCB. Next add-on per the slides?
why: Aldosterone antagonists can be added for resistant hypertension, with close potassium and renal monitoring on an ACEi/ARB.
takeaway: Fix the diuretic first, then spironolactone.
discriminator: Watch hyperkalemia.

stem: A diabetic patient on lisinopril is started on aliskiren for extra BP control. Best response?
why: Aliskiren is not combined with an ACEi or ARB — additive hyperkalemia/hypotension, no added benefit; never in diabetes.
discriminator: Aliskiren is mainly a teaching example.

stem: Why are loop diuretics the most potent class?

options.B: They are filtered but not reabsorbed
options.E: They act in the collecting duct

why: Potency tracks the share of sodium reabsorbed at the blocked segment: loop ~25%, thiazide ~6%, CAI ~4%, K⁺-sparing ~2%.

whys.E: They act at the thick ascending limb.

takeaway: Need potent natriuresis? Reach for a loop.
discriminator: Proximal agents act before the loop, so the loop compensates.

stem: Which acid–base change does acetazolamide predictably cause?
why: Blocking carbonic anhydrase causes bicarbonate diuresis and metabolic acidosis.
discriminator: Watch for kidney stones and potassium loss.
